Prayer and Fasting
PRAIR and FAS-ting
noun phrase
From Latin precari (to beg, entreat) and Old English fæstan (to abstain from food); the joining of earnest prayer with abstinence in seasons of seeking God.

Biblical Definition

Prayer and fasting is the joining of earnest, importunate prayer with the voluntary abstinence from food, that the soul may humble itself and give itself wholly to the seeking of God. Our Lord taught that certain spiritual battles yield to no lesser exercise: "Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting." Fasting is no meritorious work, and it does not bend the will of God by its own power; rather, it is the body's servant to the soul's earnestness, a setting aside of lawful comforts that the whole man may bend himself to prayer with undivided attention and self-denying gravity. The early church practiced it at every solemn juncture. When the Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work, "they had fasted and prayed" and laid their hands on them; and as they ordained elders in every church, "they prayed with fasting, and commended them to the Lord." Thus fasting accompanies the great decisions of the church—the sending of missionaries, the setting apart of officers, seasons of repentance and of seeking guidance. It is to be done not for the eyes of men but unto the Father, in lowliness and sincerity. The 1689 Confession numbers "solemn humiliations, with fastings" among the parts of religious worship to be used in a holy and religious manner. Prayer and fasting, then, is the posture of a church and a soul that means business with God—hungering after Him more than after bread.

Webster 1828 Definition

The religious exercise of joining earnest prayer with abstinence from food, practiced in seasons of solemn seeking, repentance, or important decision.

FASTING, n. From Old English fæstan, to abstain; voluntary abstinence from food joined with prayer.

The act of abstaining from food, especially as a religious duty united with prayer and humiliation.

A solemn exercise of devotion in which the body is denied that the soul may seek God the more earnestly.

Practiced by the church at solemn junctures: "they prayed with fasting, and commended them to the Lord" (Act 14:23).

Not a meritorious work, but a help to fervent prayer and an expression of humble dependence.

Key Scripture

Mat 17:21 — "Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting."

Act 13:3 — "And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away."

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Joe 2:12 — "Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning."

Modern Corruption

No postmodern redefinition assails this discipline; the abiding dangers are neglect on the one hand and a merit-seeking, outward formalism on the other.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruptions of prayer and fasting are old, not new. On one side lies simple neglect, as though the discipline belonged to a former age and had no place in the believer's life today. On the other lies the hypocrite's fast that Isaiah and our Lord both rebuked—an outward show of abstinence, paraded before men, divorced from a humbled heart and earnest prayer.

The principle to recover is that fasting is the servant of prayer, not a meritorious work—a setting aside of lawful comforts so that the whole man may seek God with undivided earnestness. Practiced unto the Father in secret, joined to importunate prayer at solemn junctures, it humbles the soul and presses it upon God. The 1689 Confession numbers solemn humiliations with fastings among the duties of worship; the church does well to keep them in seasons of repentance, decision, and the setting apart of her officers.

Hebrew Roots

The phrase pairs the act of entreaty with the act of abstinence in the service of seeking God.

expand to see more

Greek nēsteia — fasting, abstinence from food; the term in Acts and the Gospels.

Greek proseuchē — prayer; joined with fasting in Matthew 17:21.

Old English fæstan — to abstain, hold fast; source of the English "fast."

Hebrew ṣōm — to fast, to abstain from food in mourning or supplication.

Fasting accompanies the church's solemn acts: missions, ordination, repentance, and seeking guidance.

Usage

"Doctrinally, prayer and fasting belongs to the means and parts of religious worship."

"Ecclesially, it attends the sending of missionaries and the ordination of elders."

"Devotionally, it humbles the soul in seasons of repentance and earnest seeking of God."
